newsitem.title: ZAIRE: International moves quicken to avert Zaire tragedy.
newsitem.headline: International moves quicken to avert Zaire tragedy.

text.p: France and Spain have called for international support for a U.N.-sanctioned military force to avert a refugee tragedy in eastern Zaire, where rebels offered a truce after overwhelming government forces.
After two weeks of battles in which ethnic Tutsis wrested control of Zaire's two eastern provinces, Kenya also prepared to stage the first African summit on Tuesday on the conflict.

President Daniel arap Moi was due to meet leaders of Tanzania, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Zambia and Cameroon for talks on the most serious crisis in the Great Lakes region of Central Africa since the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda.
Fighting flared two weeks ago following attempts by provincial authorities backed by the army to expel Banyamulenge Tutsis whose ancestors settled from Rwanda 200 years ago.
Zaire accuses them of being surrogates of Rwanda's Tutsi army which won the civil war in 1994, sending more than one million majority Hutus fleeing into Zaire and stoking ethnic rivalries.

Zaire is boycotting the Nairobi talks but on Monday banned anti-Tutsi protests in what appeared to be a goodwill gesture. The governmemt ordered troops to open fire on anyone caught looting. Tutsi homes and property were ransacked last week.

Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko left Switzerland on Monday after three months in Lausanne, where he was operated on for cancer, and flew to the French Riviera capital of Nice. His spokesman said on Zaire television that Mobutu was expected to return home shortly.
In other diplomatic moves, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel called for a special session of the U.N. Securiuty Council on the conflict. U.N. sources said such a session was likely on Tuesday.
But the boldest move was France's championship of a military mission to help more than a million refugees, most of them Rwandan Hutus, dispersed from camps in Zaire by fighting.
France stirred controversy for a similar role in 1994 when more than a million Hutus were on the run from Rwanda after massacring up to a million minority Tutsis.
France already has troops based in several African locations and can also draw on paratroopers, Foreign Legion and Marine units based in France and used to operating in Africa.
French President Jacques Chirac won the early support of Spain for such an intervention during a summit on Monday.
Chirac and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar agreed in Marseille to "unite their efforts" and prepare a "temporary effort to ensure security" in eastern Zaire.

"The two countries will take part in an international meeting to prepare this operation to which they are prepared to contribute and which should be decided by the U.N. Security Council," the two said in a statement.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said: "What we're proposing is that the international community -- Europe, the United States, African states -- organise so that there is a security force on the ground to guarantee people's safety."
"France is willing to take part on the strict condition that there is an American, European and African participation," he said in a television interview in Marseille.
Asked whether France would send troops to Zaire, Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said: "It is a possibility which we are considering".

France's position is backed by leaders of aid organisations who say the conflict in the volatile Great Lakes region was not just a humanitarian issue but a problem requiring a political approach, including military intervention.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his fighters would observe a three-week ceasefire from 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) to allow 1.1 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees to return home.

Correspondents in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma said on Monday night the ceasefire appeared to be holding as there had been no sounds of gunfire heard since mid-morning.
